title: Mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable, practically usable way to calculate whether earthquake shaking will cause soil liquefaction and how the ground will subsequently deform. It would connect measured soil conditions and specified earthquake loading to predictions of liquefaction triggering, pore-pressure evolution, settlement and lateral spreading. Liquefaction involves the generation of pore pressure and substantial loss of soil stiffness and strength; predicting its onset and predicting the resulting ground movement are related but distinct tasks.

The intended advance is a mechanics-based predictive framework whose material descriptions remain consistent across relevant loading conditions and whose calibration is feasible with specified laboratory and in-situ measurements. Constitutive models—the mathematical descriptions of how soil responds to loading—are central to this goal. The full proposed claim would also test static foundation strength and deformation on the same soil using the same material parameters. That extension would examine constitutive consistency beyond the minimum requirement of predicting liquefaction and its consequences.

Scope synthesis: this is a prediction capability. It does not require exact simulation of every soil particle, and it does not include a method for permanently strengthening the ground. Its practical identity is a calculation that engineers can calibrate, validate and use within a demonstrated range of conditions, with explicit uncertainty.

significance.text: The revolutionary potential would come from making reliable calculations possible beyond the conditions well represented in earthquake case histories. The National Academies' 2021 report describes commonly used liquefaction-triggering methods as empirical and emphasizes that extrapolation beyond their case-history support needs laboratory evidence and soil-mechanics principles. An independently validated mechanics-based method could give engineers a stronger basis for evaluating unfamiliar conditions and understanding why a site is vulnerable.

Conditional impact synthesis: predicting both triggering and deformation could improve foundation design, evaluation of ground-treatment needs and comparison of engineering alternatives. Settlement and lateral displacement matter because a prediction that liquefaction will occur does not by itself establish the resulting damage. The direct benefit would be physically grounded estimates within a validated domain, accompanied by uncertainty that can inform design decisions.

The analogy to replacing correlations with engineering calculations has limits. Mechanics-based models still need measured inputs, calibration and validation. Success for several soil densities and shaking levels would not automatically establish reliability for additional soil types, earthquake magnitudes, depths or site configurations. The supplied National Academies chapter also treats liquefaction triggering separately from consequence assessment; it does not justify describing all existing predictions of ground movement as empirical triggering charts.

Conditional downstream possibilities include better targeting of retrofit and ground treatment, but economical city-scale intervention would require separate capabilities. Prediction alone cannot ensure adequate site characterization, construction quality or elimination of liquefaction failures. A formulation combining particle-scale prediction with cheap, permanent ground improvement would join distinct scientific and engineering goals; the historical wording and attribution referenced in the earlier research cannot be verified from the supplied material.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is dependable mechanics-based prediction that is also readily usable in engineering practice. In 2021, the National Academies identified flaws in simplified empirical triggering methods and anticipated continued heavy reliance on them until reliable, usable mechanics-based approaches became available. This establishes the documented technical goal and historical gap; it does not establish the extent to which that gap remained open across the profession in November 2026.

A central scientific barrier is obtaining a constitutive description that predicts soil behavior accurately and consistently across monotonic, cyclic and seismic loading. The reviewed Acta Geotechnica study documents condition-dependent strengths and limitations in the models it examines and calls for comprehensive validation across static and dynamic conditions. Success under one loading regime therefore cannot substitute for evidence under the others.

Engineering synthesis: the framework must connect material response and pore-pressure evolution to ground-scale settlement and lateral displacement while accounting for shaking input, geometry, drainage and boundary conditions. It must also distinguish model error from uncertainty in measurements and site characterization. A calculation that reproduces a case only after its parameters are adjusted to the observed outcome would not demonstrate the predictive capability sought here.

Practical synthesis: calibration must be sufficiently constrained and repeatable that different engineering teams can obtain useful predictions from the specified measurements. The challenge includes defining where the method is reliable, recognizing inputs outside its validated range and making uncertainty usable in design. These requirements are part of the proposed interpretation of practical reliability, rather than evidence that a particular existing model has failed them.

current_state.text: The National Academies' 2021 report, State of the Art and Practice in the Assessment of Earthquake-Induced Soil Liquefaction and Its Consequences, identified the simplified stress-based procedure of Seed and Idriss and its successors as the most commonly used approach in practice for predicting liquefaction triggering. It credited empirical methods with substantial service to the profession while identifying flaws in each and anticipating continued reliance until reliable, readily usable mechanics-based approaches became available. Its discussion distinguishes triggering assessment from the separate assessment of consequences.

Advanced constitutive modeling has demonstrated useful simulation capabilities alongside unresolved limitations. The article Advanced soil constitutive models for predicting soil-pile-superstructure interaction: evaluating liquefiable soil behavior under monotonic, cyclic, and seismic loading was published online on 15 December 2025 and appeared in a 2026 Acta Geotechnica volume. The supplied review reports successful simulations as well as significant limitations for SANISAND and the model identified as MHP with IGS, with their relative strengths depending on loading conditions. These findings support continued technical progress and the need for broader validation; they establish neither universal model failure nor a practice-wide replacement of empirical methods.

The article's discussion of remaining challenges across monotonic, cyclic and seismic loading occurs in its Introduction, rather than its Abstract as stated in the earlier research. The supplied review had substantial article prose and all 24 PDF pages available, so describing the evidence as abstract-only would understate access. However, equations and symbols contained extraction artifacts, and figures were not inspected. Consequently, numerical performance shown in figures was not independently verified in that review, and no numerical accuracy claim can be established here from those figures.

The National Academies evidence was a retained, truncated chapter rather than the complete report, and its figure content was not inspectable. The relevant passages supporting the 2021 practice assessment and mechanics-based replacement goal were retained. The chapters to which it refers for consequence assessment were not supplied, limiting conclusions about the full range of existing consequence-prediction methods.

Evidence boundary as of 1 November 2026: the supplied freshness-search record is empty. The dated sources establish the 2021 practice assessment and research published in December 2025, but do not establish subsequent practice-wide adoption or categorical nonreplacement by November 2026. This remaining uncertainty does not invalidate the documented findings or show that later advances did not occur.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: before the results of a new centrifuge benchmark or an unrevealed earthquake case are available to the prediction team, freeze the model, calibration procedure and parameters derived from specified standard laboratory and in-situ measurements. Supply the shaking input, geometry, drainage and boundary conditions needed to define the problem. Predict triggering, pore-pressure histories, settlement and lateral displacement across more than one soil density and shaking level.
completion_criteria.label: Predict liquefaction consequences blindly across soil densities and shaking levels

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance criteria: predictions should meet output-specific error limits agreed before outcomes are revealed, with measurement uncertainty included in the evaluation. No case-specific retuning should be permitted during the blind comparison. The supplied material does not specify defensible numerical tolerances, so none are asserted here. These would be benchmark requirements chosen for the intended use, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Meet preagreed output-specific error limits without case-specific retuning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed field and reproducibility checks: evaluate the frozen framework on at least one well-recorded field case withheld from calibration, and enable independent teams to reproduce calibration and prediction from the documented measurements, model version and numerical setup. Additional blind cases should test whether performance transfers beyond the original benchmark rather than merely reproducing its particular conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Validate withheld field performance and independently reproduce calibration and predictions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed full-claim extension: predict static foundation strength and deformation on the same soil using the same material parameter set. This would test consistency between seismic and non-seismic behavior. Predicting liquefaction consequences remains the minimum convincing scope; a ground-improvement method is outside the demonstration. The cross-loading extension is motivated by the reviewed article's emphasis on validation under diverse static and dynamic conditions, but its exact test design is a proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Predict static foundation behavior using identical material parameters

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report the tested soil states, loading conditions, geometries, drainage assumptions, input uncertainty and calibration effort alongside the results. A convincing demonstration would establish reproducible performance across that domain. Finite successful tests establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality; claims for additional soil types, depths, magnitudes or configurations would require further evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Report demonstrated validity domain, input uncertainty and calibration effort

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison—CIV-03, In-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid, has the closest relationship. CIV-02 predicts soil response; CIV-03 concerns changing the ground's engineering properties. Prediction could help specify treatment needs or evaluate treated ground if validated for those materials, but it does not supply the treatment process. Only CIV-03's title was supplied, so its detailed mechanism and intended relationship to liquefaction remain unverified.

Roster-based comparison—CIV-09, Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost, and CIV-12, Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost, share the objective of better earthquake performance. CIV-02 addresses ground and foundation hazards that can constrain those objectives. Immediate occupancy and adaptive structural response nevertheless require building-level capabilities beyond predicting soil behavior.

Roster-based comparison—CIV-06, Underground routes and spaces at surface-infrastructure cost, could benefit from better ground-response assessment where liquefaction is relevant. Its defining challenge is the cost and delivery of underground infrastructure, which mechanics-based liquefaction prediction alone would not resolve.

Roster-based comparison—CIV-01, A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide; CIV-05, Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost; and CIV-11, Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures, concern construction materials and their production, mechanical behavior or durability. They may be used in foundations and infrastructure exposed to ground movement, but their defining advances remain separate from predicting that movement.

Roster-based comparison—CIV-04, Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking; CIV-07, Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures; and CIV-10, Structural concrete that stores building-relevant energy, concern recovery or additional functions of structural materials. CIV-02 could provide ground-deformation demands relevant to their applications, without supplying their recovery, living-material or energy-storage capabilities.

Roster-based comparison—CIV-08, Large-reservoir storage that passes sediment without giving up carryover water, addresses a distinct reservoir-function problem. Liquefaction prediction could be relevant to seismic evaluation of associated earthworks, but it would not establish sediment passage or preservation of carryover storage. These comparisons preserve the roster's separate concepts and infer relationships only from the supplied titles.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-02's ID, title and central prediction capability while separating triggering, pore-pressure evolution and ground deformation.
change_log.reason: The review supports the concept but identifies triggering and consequence assessment as distinct technical tasks.

change_log.change: Dated the empirical-method prevalence assessment to 2021 and removed the categorical claim that mechanics-based methods had not become a replacement by November 2026.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources and empty freshness-search record do not establish practice-wide adoption at the later date.

change_log.change: Retained the 2025 study's successful simulations alongside its condition-dependent model limitations.
change_log.reason: Omitting demonstrated successes would misrepresent the reviewed evidence and imply broader failure than the study establishes.

change_log.change: Corrected the article's challenge-statement location to the Introduction, distinguished its December 2025 online publication from its 2026 volume, and replaced the abstract-only access description.
change_log.reason: The review had substantial article prose and a complete 24-page PDF, although figures were uninspected and equation extraction had artifacts.

change_log.change: Expanded blind validation to specify necessary inputs, freeze calibration procedures and parameters, account for uncertainty, and include independent reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish prospective prediction from retrospective fitting and make the proposed demonstration assessable.

change_log.change: Kept static foundation prediction as a full-claim extension and liquefaction consequences as the minimum demonstration scope.
change_log.reason: Cross-loading consistency is scientifically useful but exceeds the minimum liquefaction prediction capability.

change_log.change: Bounded the impact claim and proposed validation to independently tested conditions.
change_log.reason: A finite benchmark cannot establish applicability to arbitrary soils, magnitudes, depths or configurations.

change_log.change: Separated prediction from ground improvement and converted the historical formulation and CIV-03 relationship into qualified comparisons.
change_log.reason: The historical entry and detailed CIV-03 material were absent; only the roster title supports the conceptual distinction.

change_log.change: Added substantive related-concept comparisons across the supplied roster and preserved source-access limitations.
change_log.reason: The final record must stand alone without merging distinct innovations or implying evidence beyond the supplied review.

unresolved_issues: Whether mechanics-based methods had become a reliable, readily usable replacement across engineering practice by 1 November 2026 remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
Numerical accuracy and detailed performance comparisons in the 2025 article's figures were not independently verified in the supplied review; equation and symbol extraction also had artifacts.
The supplied National Academies chapter does not establish the full state of consequence-prediction practice because the referenced consequence chapters were not supplied.
Output-specific acceptance tolerances, measurement-uncertainty treatment and the intended initial validation domain remain to be defined for the proposed demonstration.
The historical formulation's exact wording and attribution remain unverified, and CIV-03's detailed scope cannot be established from its roster title alone.

brief.title: Predicting earthquake soil failure and ground movement
possible: Engineers could reliably calculate when earthquake shaking will make soil lose stiffness and strength—a process called liquefaction—and how far the ground will sink or move sideways. The calculation would connect soil measurements and expected shaking to consequences for foundations.
why: Engineers could assess unfamiliar conditions with a stronger physical basis than comparisons with past earthquakes alone. Predicting ground movement as well as soil failure would help them compare foundation designs and decide where ground treatment is needed.

sources.who: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sources.showed: Their assessment identified methods based on past earthquakes as the most commonly used way to predict liquefaction onset. It found flaws in these methods and called for soil mechanics and laboratory data to support predictions beyond past cases.
sources.quote: Only the specific adjustment factors used for development of a particular liquefaction triggering relationship are suitable for use with that relationship.
sources.cited_for: The need for predictions grounded in soil mechanics when past earthquake cases do not cover the conditions.
sources.not_established: The assessment does not demonstrate a reliable, practical calculation of both soil failure and subsequent ground movement.

sources.who: Mehdi Joneidi, Gertraud Medicus and colleagues
sources.showed: They compared mathematical models of soil response with laboratory and model-scale shaking tests. A model called SANISAND captured structural response but overpredicted water pressure between soil grains; their modified model improved pressure and acceleration predictions.
sources.quote: SANISAND is effective in predicting the superstructure response; however, it overestimates pore water pressure accumulation.
sources.cited_for: Soil-response models can reproduce useful aspects of shaking behavior, but their strengths depend on the conditions.
sources.not_established: These comparisons do not establish reliable predictions of soil failure and ground movement across unfamiliar sites and loading conditions.

shown: Joneidi and colleagues improved simulations of water pressure and acceleration in tests involving soil, foundation piles and a structure. Their comparisons also exposed weaknesses that varied with the loading conditions. Consistent performance across steady loading, repeated loading and earthquake shaking remains a challenge.
missing: A soil-response model must predict both liquefaction and ground movement consistently across relevant loading conditions.
Blind tests must demonstrate useful accuracy without adjusting the model after the outcomes are known.
Independent teams must reproduce calibration—the fitting of model settings to soil measurements—and predictions with practical effort.

milestones.label: Blind predictions across soil densities and shaking levels
milestones.explanation: A model fixed using specified soil measurements would have to predict failure, water pressure, sinking and sideways movement before outcomes are revealed, across densities and shaking levels. This would test prediction without hindsight.

milestones.label: Agreed accuracy without adjusting settings for each case
milestones.explanation: Predictions would have to meet error limits agreed for each output, allowing for measurement uncertainty and without adjusting settings for each case. This would establish whether accuracy meets the intended use.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction and success on withheld field cases
milestones.explanation: The fixed model would have to predict a field case excluded from calibration, with independent teams reproducing calibration and predictions. Further blind cases would test whether success extends beyond the original benchmark.

milestones.label: Stronger test: foundation behavior with identical soil settings
milestones.explanation: The same soil settings would have to predict foundation strength and deformation under steady loads on the same soil. This would test consistency beyond earthquake behavior, extending the minimum goal of predicting liquefaction consequences.

milestones.label: Clear limits, input uncertainty and calibration effort
milestones.explanation: Results would have to state tested soils, loads, geometries, drainage conditions, input uncertainty and calibration effort. This would define where reproducible performance has been demonstrated and what practical use requires.

uncertain: The acceptable error for each predicted outcome, and how measurement uncertainty should affect acceptance, remain to be defined.
The initial range of soils and site conditions that would count as a convincing demonstration remains to be defined.
How well successful predictions would transfer to other soils, depths, earthquake sizes and site configurations remains open.
